subject: Biology
lessonIntent: *How do prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ, and how do we know?*

scenes.title: hook (a stained cheek cell)

voiceover.text: Put a prepared, stained slide of cheek cells under a light microscope. You'll see big, flat cells, each with a dark dot near the middle. Look closely at their edges, and you might spot tiny specks stuck to them. Those specks are bacteria from your mouth. Both are alive, releasing energy and making proteins. Yet they're built in two completely different ways. So how do the two cell types differ, and how do we actually know?

scenes.sourceVisual: no people. New y11-cheek-cell-bacteria-v1.png fades up inside a coded circular microscope field (soft vignette): two stained cheek cells, pale blue, each with a darker nucleus, with a few tiny rod bacteria on their surfaces. On "big, flat cells" a callout to one cheek cell, label "cheek cell". On "a dark dot" a small scribbleEllipse circles its nucleus (no label yet). On "two completely different ways" the camera pulls back and the two labels pulse. On the question the heading writes: "How do prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ?" At most three bright text items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: the dividing question

voiceover.text: One question splits every cell ever found into two groups: is the cell's DNA wrapped inside its own membrane? When a membrane surrounds something, we call that thing membrane-bound. In your cheek cell, the DNA sits inside a membrane-bound nucleus. That makes it a eukaryote. In the bacterium, there's no nucleus. Its DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid. That makes it a prokaryote.

scenes.sourceVisual: the field shrinks to a thumbnail at the upper left. The two-cell bench sets up: m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png at the left, m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png at the right, each about 45 per cent of frame height (not to scale with each other; grey tag "not to scale" at the bottom centre, until scene 6). On the question a handwritten line writes across the top: "Is the DNA wrapped in its own membrane?" On "When a membrane surrounds something" a bright DrawPath traces the eukaryote's nuclear envelope once (never the outer cell membrane, which the bacterium also has), gloss "membrane-bound: wrapped in a membrane". On "membrane-bound nucleus" the traced envelope brightens and the nucleus fills with a soft highlight; label "nucleus (DNA inside)". On "eukaryote" a large handwritten label "EUKARYOTE" writes above the right cell. On "no nucleus" the Cam moves to the bacterium and a scribbleEllipse circles its tangled DNA; on "nucleoid" the label "nucleoid: DNA, no membrane around it" writes. On "prokaryote" "PROKARYOTE" writes above the left cell. At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: who's who, and the shared kit

voiceover.text: All bacteria are prokaryotes. Animals, plants, fungi like yeast, and single-celled protists are built from eukaryotic cells. But here's the important part. Every cell, of either type, has the same basic kit: a cell membrane around it, cytoplasm, the jelly-like fluid inside, ribosomes, which build proteins, and DNA, which carries the instructions. So the difference isn't what's inside. It's how it's organised.

scenes.sourceVisual: the bench stays. On "All bacteria" a small grey tag under PROKARYOTE: "bacteria (also archaea)". On "Animals, plants, fungi like yeast" three small thumbnails slide in under EUKARYOTE in a row: the cheek cell (cropped from the hook plate), b6a-plant-cell-v1.png, y11-budding-yeast-v1.png, each with a grey tag ("animal", "plant", "fungus: yeast"); on "protists" a fourth grey text tag "protists" (no plate). On "same basic kit" the thumbnails leave and four paired callouts draw on both cells at once, one per cue: "cell membrane" (both outlines trace), "cytoplasm" (both interiors tint), "ribosomes" (a few dots on each pulse), "DNA" (the nucleoid tangle and the nucleus both glow). On "how it's organised" the coded comparison ledger strip draws along the bottom with headings "Feature | Prokaryotic | Eukaryotic" and its first row writes, spanning both columns: "Shared: membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: DNA shape

voiceover.text: Start with the DNA itself. A prokaryote usually has one circular chromosome, a single loop of DNA, lying in the nucleoid. Many also carry plasmids, small extra rings of DNA. A eukaryote has several long, straight chromosomes, and they're kept inside the nucleus, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear membrane, also called the nuclear envelope.

scenes.sourceVisual: the Cam pushes in on the bacterium. A coded overlay simplifies its tangle: one bright closed loop draws through the nucleoid, label "one circular chromosome". On "plasmids" a callout to the small ring already painted at the right end, label "plasmid: small extra ring". The camera moves to the eukaryote and pushes in on the nucleus; four coded straight threads of different lengths draw inside it (open ends visible), label "several linear chromosomes". On "nuclear envelope" the envelope traces bright, label "nuclear envelope (two membranes)". On "nuclear envelope" (after its label) the camera pulls back to the bench and the ring and the threads pulse in turn. The ledger adds a row: "DNA | one circular chromosome, free; often plasmids | several linear chromosomes, in a nucleus". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: compartments

voiceover.text: Next, compartments. A eukaryotic cell is divided up by internal membranes into organelles, small structures that each do one job, such as mitochondria, which release energy from glucose. Each membrane keeps its own contents and conditions apart, so reactions that would clash can run at the same time in separate spaces. A prokaryote like this one has no nucleus and none of those organelles. It runs its reactions in the cytoplasm and on the inside of its cell membrane. That doesn't make it primitive. Bacteria carry out every process of life.

scenes.sourceVisual: the camera moves to the eukaryote. On "internal membranes" bright DrawPath outlines trace the rough ER, the Golgi stack and one mitochondrion in turn; label "organelles: membrane-bound compartments". On "mitochondria" a callout to a mitochondrion, label "mitochondrion: energy released from glucose". On "contents and conditions apart" two of the traced compartments tint in two different colours (coded, low opacity) with a tiny coded dot cluster inside each that stays inside its own boundary. On "no nucleus and none of those organelles" the camera moves to the bacterium; a grey chip "this bacterium: no nucleus or eukaryotic organelles" (Revision 3: cue retied to the spoken phrase). On "in the cytoplasm and on the inside of its cell membrane" the bacterium's cytoplasm tints and its inner membrane edge glows. On "primitive" a grey chip "prokaryotes are primitive" writes and takes a scribble cross; on "every process of life" the hook's two chips ("release energy", "make proteins") return small beside the bacterium with ticks. The ledger adds a row: "Membrane-bound organelles | none | many (e.g. mitochondria)". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: size

voiceover.text: Then size. Most prokaryotic cells are about one to five micrometres long. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. Eukaryotic cells are usually about ten to a hundred micrometres across. So a typical eukaryotic cell is around ten times wider, and because volume grows in all three directions, that's roughly a thousand times more volume. Diagrams often draw the two cells the same size. They're not even close.

scenes.sourceVisual: the "not to scale" tag takes a scribble cross. On "one to five micrometres" a coded ScaleBar draws under the bacterium, "5 µm"; gloss "1 µm = 1/1000 mm". On "ten to a hundred micrometres" the bench rescales to true relative size: the eukaryote plate keeps its size while the bacterium plate shrinks uniformly to scale beside it (one named pair: a 5 µm bacterium beside a 50 µm eukaryotic cell, drawn at exactly 1 : 10 width, matching the spoken "ten times wider"); the ScaleBar now reads "50 µm" across the eukaryote, with the bacterium's "5 µm" bar kept. On "ten times wider" a coded cube of side 1 and a cube of side 10 (built from small cubes, abstract) draw at the right, labels "1 × 1 × 1" and "10 × 10 × 10"; on "a thousand times more volume" the big cube fills with a count "1000". On "draw the two cells the same size" the bench briefly snaps back to equal sizes with a grey tag "a typical diagram", then on "not even close" returns to true scale, and the hook plate returns small beside it as a real view (the rods on the cheek cell). Grey tag at the lower right: "why prokaryotes stay small: Focus Area 2". The ledger adds a row: "Size | about 1 to 5 µm | about 10 to 100 µm". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: ribosomes

voiceover.text: Both cell types have ribosomes, but they're not identical. Prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller, labelled 70S, and eukaryotic ribosomes are larger, labelled 80S. The S describes how fast they settle when spun at very high speed. That small difference matters. Some antibiotics jam the 70S ribosomes of bacteria, so the bacteria can't make proteins, while your own 80S ribosomes keep working.

scenes.sourceVisual: the bench returns to the two-cell layout (not to scale; tag back). On "Both cell types have ribosomes" ribosome dots in both cells pulse and two callouts lead to an enlarged inset: m5x-ribosome-v1.png twice, the left copy scaled uniformly to about 80 per cent of the right; labels "70S (prokaryote)" and "80S (eukaryote)". On "settle when spun" a coded spinning-tube icon (abstract outline) with a small grey tag "S: settling speed in a centrifuge". On "Some antibiotics" a coded pill outline (abstract) slides onto the 70S ribosome and a small coded block sits in its groove; the bacterium's protein-making chip ("make proteins") greys out with a small cross. On "your own 80S ribosomes keep working" the 80S copy glows and its chip stays ticked. The ledger adds a row: "Ribosomes | smaller (70S) | larger (80S)". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: how we know

voiceover.text: So how do we know all this? A light microscope can't separate two points closer than about two hundred nanometres. A nanometre is a thousandth of a micrometre. So it shows a cell and its nucleus, but not the thin membranes inside. Electron microscopes show far finer detail, and they revealed that typical prokaryotes have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. That's why scientists use a variety of sources: micrographs, which are microscope photos, labelled diagrams, and tables of measurements. Each can mislead on its own, so they're checked against each other.

scenes.sourceVisual: the bench and ledger dim to the lower third. y11-microscopy-pair-v1.png enters at the centre, cropped by Cam to its light microscope half first. On "about two hundred nanometres" two coded dots draw close together and blur into one; label "light microscope: limit about 200 nm"; gloss "1 nm = 1/1000 µm". On "a cell and its nucleus" a callout to the light-microscope field's cells and their nuclei. The camera moves to the electron microscope half; on "far finer detail" a callout to its field showing internal membranes, label "electron microscope: far finer detail (video 7)". On "variety of sources" three small cards slide in, one per cue: "micrograph" (the light field thumbnail), "labelled diagram" (the bench's equal-size bacterium and cell, tiny), "table of measurements" (a coded two-row table: "prokaryote 1 to 5 µm", "eukaryote 10 to 100 µm"). On "checked against each other" coded double-headed arrows draw between the three cards. At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: comparing properly

voiceover.text: When a question says compare, give both cell types on the same feature, in the same sentence, and include what they share. So, both have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA. A eukaryote's DNA is in a nucleus, whereas a prokaryote's lies free in the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles, whereas prokaryotes have none. And prokaryotes are much smaller, with smaller ribosomes. Two separate paragraphs leave the comparing to the marker.

scenes.sourceVisual: the board clears to the full comparison ledger at the centre, all five rows from scenes 3 to 7. On "same feature, in the same sentence" a bright bracket joins the two cells of one row. On "include what they share" the shared row glows. Then one row at a time, on each spoken sentence, the row glows and a handwritten connector "whereas" writes between its two cells (amber), earlier rows dimming. On "Two separate paragraphs" a small grey sketch of two separate text blocks, labelled "prokaryotes ..." and "eukaryotes ...", writes at the right and takes a scribble cross; tag "a Describe answer, not a Compare". At most three bright items. Hold one second.

scenes.title: memory

voiceover.text: Two things to remember. The names come from karyon, Greek for kernel, meaning the nucleus, so a prokaryote is the one without a nucleus. And for the primitive trap: no walls inside, meaning no nucleus or organelle membranes, doesn't mean no work. An open-plan office still gets the job done.

scenes.sourceVisual: the board clears to two handwritten lines, large: "karyon = kernel (nucleus): pro-karyote, no nucleus" with the bacterium thumbnail; and "No walls inside ≠ no work: an open-plan office still gets the job done", with a small grey gloss under "walls inside": "no nucleus or organelle membranes, not the cell wall". Hold half a second.

scenes.title: attempt one (a described micrograph)

voiceover.text: Two exam questions. First. An electron micrograph shows a cell three micrometres long. It has no nuclear envelope, ribosomes throughout its cytoplasm, and a single circular DNA molecule. Identify the cell type, and justify your answer using two pieces of evidence from the micrograph. Pause here to answer.

scenes.sourceVisual: the board clears. The card writes on as an exam question, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "An electron micrograph shows a cell 3 µm long with no nuclear envelope, ribosomes throughout the cytoplasm and a single circular DNA molecule." Demand: "Identify the cell type and justify your answer using two pieces of evidence from the micrograph. (3 marks)" Lined answer space. No plates, no people. The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

scenes.title: feedback, item one

voiceover.text: It's prokaryotic. No nuclear envelope means the DNA isn't enclosed in a nucleus, and that's the defining feature. The single circular DNA molecule, and a length of three micrometres, inside the one to five range, both support it. The classic mistake is using the ribosomes as evidence. Every cell has ribosomes, so they don't tell you either way.

scenes.sourceVisual: the card stays. On "It's prokaryotic" an answer line writes "prokaryotic cell". On "No nuclear envelope" that given takes an amber underline and a line writes "no nuclear envelope → DNA not in a nucleus (defining feature)". On "single circular DNA molecule" and "three micrometres" those givens take amber underlines and a line writes "circular DNA; 3 µm (within 1 to 5 µm)"; earlier lines dim. On "classic mistake" the given "ribosomes throughout the cytoplasm" takes a thin grey underline and a chip "ribosomes show it's a prokaryote" writes and takes a scribble cross, with small text "all cells have ribosomes". Settle one second.

scenes.title: attempt two (one diagram, one claim)

voiceover.text: Second. A textbook diagram shows a bacterium and a human cheek cell side by side, drawn the same size. A student concludes that the two cells are about the same size. Explain why this conclusion is not reliable, and name another source that could check it, saying what that source would show. Pause here to answer.

scenes.sourceVisual: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "A textbook diagram shows a bacterium and a human cheek cell side by side, drawn the same size. A student concludes that the two cells are about the same size." Beside the stem, a small simplified diagram: the bench's two plates at equal size inside a thin frame, labelled "bacterium" and "cheek cell" (no scale bar). Demand: "(a) Explain why the student's conclusion is not reliable. (2 marks) (b) Name another source that could check the conclusion, and state what it would show. (2 marks)" The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card, diagram included, stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

scenes.title: feedback, item two

voiceover.text: Diagrams are drawn for clarity, not to scale, so one diagram can't tell you real size. A micrograph with a scale bar, or a table of measured sizes, would check it. It would show the bacterium at about one to five micrometres, and the cheek cell around ten times longer or more. The classic mistake is trusting the diagram because it's labelled. Labels name the parts, they don't measure them.

scenes.sourceVisual: the card stays. On "not to scale" the given "drawn the same size" takes an amber underline and an answer line writes "(a) diagram drawn for clarity, not to scale → can't show real size". On "A micrograph with a scale bar" the hook plate appears small beside the card with a coded ScaleBar "10 µm"; on "a table of measured sizes" the coded two-row size table from scene 8 appears under it; a line writes "(b) micrograph with scale bar, or measured sizes: bacterium about 1 to 5 µm, cheek cell about 10 times longer or more". On "classic mistake" the diagram's labels take a thin grey underline and a chip "it's labelled, so it's accurate" writes and takes a scribble cross. Settle one second.

scenes.title: decision rule and handoff

voiceover.text: So, to classify any cell, look for the nucleus first: DNA inside its own membrane means eukaryote. Then check the supporting clues, and more than one source. Next, we'll go inside a eukaryotic cell and see what each organelle does.

scenes.sourceVisual: three step chips write on, one per cue: "DNA in a membrane-bound nucleus? → eukaryote", "supporting clues: DNA shape, organelles, size, ribosomes", "check more than one source". The two-cell bench returns small above them at true scale. On "Next" the chips and the bacterium leave and m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png moves to the centre at about 60 per cent of frame height; a "Next" chip slides in at the lower right: "Next: Inside the eukaryotic cell: what does each organelle do?" The camera begins a slow push towards the nucleus. This is the handoff frame; v02 opens from it. Hold half a second before the notes.
